title: William James
summary: William James was an American philosopher and psychologist and one of the founders of pragmatism. He believed ideas should be tested by the difference they make in life, and he was one of the first to describe consciousness as a living, continuous “stream.” Having gone through a severe emotional crisis in his youth, he wrote about inner life with rare compassion.
onEmotions: James proposed a famous theory, known as the James–Lange theory: an emotion is, to a large extent, the feeling of bodily changes. We don't simply cry because we are sad: the sensation of tears, breathing and tension is itself a large part of sadness. Hence a practical conclusion: through the body, attention and action we can influence our feelings. James also wrote a great deal about habit, about belief, and about the “sick soul” — people who feel the dark side of life keenly — and considered their experience no less valuable than that of natural optimists.

anxiety.text: Anxiety is a hard state, and James knew it firsthand: in his youth he went through a deep emotional crisis with attacks of fear. His theory of emotions points to something important: anxiety lives largely in the body — a racing heart, uneven breathing, tense muscles. This doesn't mean it isn't “real.” But it does mean the body is not only the place where anxiety is felt, but also a door through which it can be influenced. In his essay “The Gospel of Relaxation,” James advised acting and speaking “as if” the state you want were already there. From this point of view, you can start by breathing and moving more calmly. Anxiety won't vanish on command, but its bodily basis can loosen a little — and the feeling itself grows quieter.
anxiety.practice: Place your palm on your chest or belly and take five slow breaths, making each exhale a little longer than the inhale. Notice what changes in your body — and in the feeling.

fear.text: Fear is one of the most ancient feelings, and it protects us. In his theory of emotions James put forward an unusual idea. We usually think that first we get scared and then we tremble. He believed the opposite: the body reacts first — the heart pounds, the muscles tense — and fear is to a large extent the feeling of these changes. This doesn't make fear a mistake: the body instantly assesses danger and prepares us for it. But it helps us deal with it. Fear is not a verdict that you are a coward but a wave of bodily reaction with a beginning and an end. You can notice it, name it and wait it out without merging with it: “my body is preparing for danger right now.”
fear.practice: When fear comes, say to yourself: “My body is trying to protect me right now.” Notice three bodily sensations and watch how they change.

quote.text: We feel sorry because we cry, angry because we strike, afraid because we tremble.
quote.author: William James
quote.source: The Principles of Psychology, ch. XXV “The Emotions” (1890)

sadness.text: Sadness is a legitimate feeling, and James had great respect for people who feel it keenly. In The Varieties of Religious Experience he distinguished the “healthy-minded” — natural optimists — from the “sick soul” — people who deeply feel the sorrowful side of life. Despite the name, he didn't consider the latter worse off: on the contrary, in his view their experience is broader, because it takes into account everything in the world, including pain. From this point of view, your sadness is not an error of perception but a way of seeing reality more deeply. James wrote that such people, having passed through darkness, often arrive at a more lasting joy — he called them the “twice-born.” Sadness can be part of that path rather than a dead end.
sadness.practice: Write down what your sadness allows you to see or understand — something people who have never been sad might not notice.

grief.text: Grief is one of the deepest experiences, and it can't be “fixed” with advice. James understood this well. His theory of emotions shows how closely feelings are tied to the body: grief is felt as heaviness in the chest, a lump in the throat, tiredness — and this is not weakness but a living organism's natural response to loss. In The Principles of Psychology he wrote that the people close to us become part of our “self,” and when they go, a part of us goes with them. From this point of view, it's clear why grief also feels like a loss of oneself. This is natural. From a pragmatic point of view, small everyday actions can be something to lean on: they help life go on while the feeling is lived through at its own pace.
grief.practice: Choose one small action that will support your body today: a glass of water, a short walk, a warm meal. Let the grief be while you take care of yourself.

loneliness.text: Loneliness is a painful feeling, and James would explain why it wounds so deeply. In The Principles of Psychology he described the “social self” — the part of our self that lives in the recognition of others. He wrote that a person has as many social selves as there are individuals who recognize them and carry an image of them in their minds. And he observed that hardly any punishment more cruel could be devised than to be turned loose in society and remain absolutely unnoticed. From this point of view, loneliness is not a whim but the hunger of a very important part of you. This helps you accept the feeling without shame. James's pragmatism also suggests a direction: look not at all your connections at once, but at what small step toward someone is possible today.
loneliness.practice: Think of one person who probably remembers you and thinks of you warmly. What small sign of attention could you send them?

anger.text: Anger is a strong feeling, and there is often truth in it: something has touched your boundaries or values. Starting from his theory of emotions, James noticed that the bodily expression of a feeling largely feeds it. In The Principles of Psychology he wrote that if you count ten before venting your anger, its occasion may come to seem quite different. From this point of view, one could say there is a space between the flare-up and the action. It isn't about pretending there is no anger — James, in fact, showed that feelings are real and bodily. It's about letting the body calm down a little and then calmly deciding what you want to do about what made you angry. Anger then becomes information rather than a command.
anger.practice: When you feel anger, slowly count to ten, noticing your breath. Then ask: what exactly touched me, and what do I want to do about it?

shame.text: Shame is a very painful feeling, and it is not your fault. James proposed a simple but deep formula: self-esteem equals our successes divided by our pretensions. That is, we suffer not simply from failures but from the gap between what we have achieved and what we expected of ourselves. He gave the example of a man who is ashamed that he is only the second-best in the world at his craft — even though almost everyone else falls short of him. From this point of view, shame can be reduced not only by increasing the “numerator” — successes — but also by revisiting the “denominator”: the demands you have taken on. James wrote that to give up some pretensions is as blessed a relief as to have them gratified.
shame.practice: Write down one demand you make of yourself that makes you feel ashamed. Whose demand is it really — and could you lower it even a little?

quote.author: William James
quote.source: The Principles of Psychology, ch. X “The Consciousness of Self” (1890)

guilt.text: Guilt is a heavy feeling, and it often shows that acting well matters to you. As a pragmatist, James looked at ideas and feelings with a question: what difference does this make in life? From this point of view, one could say that guilt is useful when it leads to action — an apology, a repair, a new habit — and becomes barren when it just goes round in circles. James valued habit highly: he wrote that our character is largely built out of many small repeated actions. So making amends doesn't require instantly turning into a different person: it's enough to take a first step and repeat it. James advised seizing the very first opportunity to act on a new resolution.
guilt.practice: What one small action could you take today in response to your guilt — not as punishment, but as repair?

envy.text: Envy is an unpleasant feeling, but it tells us a lot about ourselves. In The Principles of Psychology James described a person's self very broadly: it includes not only the body and thoughts but also clothes, home, family, work, reputation. Everything we call “mine” becomes part of us. From this point of view, envy is when someone else's “mine” touches ours: as if another person has a piece of the self we would like to have. James also noted that no one can be everything at once. He admitted with humor that he would like to be handsome, an athlete, rich, a wit, a philosopher and a saint — but having chosen one self, you have to give up the others. Envy can remind you of your choice and its value.
envy.practice: Which of the many possible selves have you chosen for yourself? Write down what is valuable to you in this choice, even if it rules something else out.

emptiness.text: Emptiness and apathy are very hard states, and James knew them personally. In his youth he went through a long crisis when life seemed meaningless and he had no strength to act. What helped him out of it, among other things, was a thought he wrote in his diary: his first act of free will could be to believe in free will. From this point of view, one could say that sometimes you don't need to wait for meaning to appear before you begin to act: a small action can itself become the beginning of meaning. This echoes his idea of “the will to believe”: in some matters our belief and our steps help create what we believe in. James promised no quick solutions, but he showed that even a tiny choice brings back the sense of taking part in your own life.
emptiness.practice: Choose one very small action you will take within the next hour simply because you decided to. Notice how it feels.

quote.text: My first act of free will shall be to believe in free will.
quote.author: William James

confusion.text: Confusion is a natural state when thoughts and feelings get tangled and there is no clear answer. James described consciousness as a “stream”: it isn't made of neat separate pieces but flows continuously, sometimes in quick “flights,” sometimes in slow “perchings.” In this stream there is always a “fringe” — vague sensations, half-thoughts, premonitions we can't yet name. From this point of view, confusion is not a malfunction but a moment when the stream has a lot of fringe and few clear resting places. This is a normal part of how the mind works. James's pragmatism adds a piece of advice: if it's unclear which thought is right, ask what practical difference each option would make. Clarity often comes not in the head but in action.
confusion.practice: Write out all the thoughts spinning in your head, without ordering them. Then for each one ask: what difference does it make to what I will do tomorrow?

fatigue.text: Tiredness and burnout are an honest signal that your strength has become less than what's demanded of you. In his essay “The Gospel of Relaxation” (1899), James noticed that many people live in constant overstrain: they hurry, tense their muscles, face and voice, even when there's no need. According to his theory of emotions, such bodily tension itself feeds the feeling of anxiety and exhaustion. From this point of view, one could say that burnout is not only a lot of work but also a habit of always being keyed up. James advised learning to let tension go: relaxing the body, not wasting energy on needless hurry, allowing yourself pauses. This isn't laziness but sensible care for a resource that isn't infinite.
fatigue.practice: Move your attention through your body: forehead, jaw, shoulders, hands. Where are you tense for no reason? On an exhale, try to let at least one place go.

boredom.text: Boredom is unpleasant, and in it the world often seems to have gone flat. James wrote a great deal about attention and habit. He showed that habit saves energy: repeated actions become automatic, and we stop noticing them. This is useful, but there is a flip side — life can turn into a background we don't look at. From this point of view, one could say that boredom is not necessarily a “boring world” but attention sliding over the familiar. James also noted that interest is born from connecting something new with what we already care about. So boredom can be met with curiosity: find one unnoticed detail in the familiar and connect it with what matters to you.
boredom.practice: Choose something familiar — a route, a room, a cup — and find three details in it you had never noticed before.

quote.text: My experience is what I agree to attend to.
quote.author: William James
quote.source: The Principles of Psychology, ch. XI “Attention” (1890)

joy.text: Joy is a wonderful feeling, and you can simply let it be. Studying emotions, James showed how joy takes hold of the whole body: lightness, squared shoulders, a smile, the urge to move. For him these are not secondary “expressions” but the very fabric of the feeling. From this point of view, one could say that joy doesn't only come to us — we can support it a little through the body: notice the smile, not hurry to hide it, let it last. In The Varieties of Religious Experience, James described with interest people of a “healthy-minded” outlook, who know how to notice the good and give themselves to it. In his view, this can partly be learned — through attention and a habit of noticing.
joy.practice: When you feel joy, stay in it for three breaths: where do you feel it in your body? Let it grow just a little.

love.text: Love and tenderness are among the strongest experiences, and James helps us see how bodily and real they are. From the standpoint of his theory of emotions, tenderness is a whole complex of sensations: warmth in the chest, softness in the face, the wish to touch. It is not an illusion but a living response of the whole organism. In The Principles of Psychology James also wrote that the people we love become part of our extended self: we experience their joys and troubles almost as our own. From this point of view, tenderness is the feeling that the boundary of your self has widened to include someone else. This makes us more vulnerable, but also richer. Pragmatism would add: love reveals itself in the difference it makes — in words, care, small acts.
love.practice: Think of someone you love and notice where in your body the tenderness responds. What small action could express it today?

gratitude.text: Gratitude is a warm feeling, and James helps us understand how to sustain it. He wrote little about gratitude directly, but from the standpoint of his psychology one could say the following. First, emotion lives in the body: gratitude is warmth, relaxation, sometimes tears, and it's worth not skipping past it but feeling it through. Second, our experience is made of what we pay attention to: if you notice the good, the world really does become different for you. Third, James believed habits are formed by repetition. Gratitude, too, can become a habit — not out of duty, but because the mind gradually learns to see what supports you. This doesn't cancel difficulties, but it adds to the picture what is already there.
gratitude.practice: Before sleep, write down one thing you are grateful for today, and for a couple of seconds feel where that gratitude is in your body.

hope.text: Hope helps us live, and James saw it not as naivety but as an important life force. In his essay “The Will to Believe” he argued that in some matters we have the right to believe even without conclusive evidence — especially when the belief itself affects the outcome. He gave the example of a mountain climber who has to leap across a chasm: confidence that the leap will succeed itself helps to make it. From this point of view, hope is not self-deception but taking part in creating the future: it gives you strength to act, and actions change reality. Hope doesn't guarantee an outcome. But it makes the step possible — and James believed that it is in this step that our freedom shows itself.
hope.practice: Finish the sentence: “If I believe this is possible, my first small step will be…”

quote.text: Believe that life is worth living, and your belief will help create the fact.
quote.author: William James
quote.source: “Is Life Worth Living?” (1895), in The Will to Believe (1897)

nostalgia.text: Nostalgia is a warm longing for the past, and James helps us understand where that warmth comes from. In The Principles of Psychology he asked: why do I recognize my past experiences as my own? And he answered: they come back in memory with a particular “warmth and intimacy” that other people's stories lack. From this point of view, one could say that nostalgia is the feeling of that very warmth, a sense of the continuity of your self. The stream of consciousness flows, everything changes, and yet you remain yourself — the past is felt as your own. Nostalgia then is not only longing for what is lost but also confirmation that your life is one story. And this warmth can be carried into the present, not only sought behind you.
nostalgia.practice: Recall a warm past experience and find something in today that continues the same thread — a taste, a person, a habit.

craving.text: A sharp craving — “I want it right now” — can be almost physical, and there's no need to be ashamed of it. James thought a lot about such moments. In The Principles of Psychology he described a struggle between two ideas in consciousness: one pulls toward a familiar pleasure, the other toward what you want for yourself as a whole. He considered attention decisive: will, for James, is largely the effort of holding the right thought before your mind until the wave subsides. And in The Varieties of Religious Experience he soberly noted that the pull toward intoxication often hides a thirst for something greater — expansion, union, a “yes” to the world — which intoxication itself fulfills only briefly and at a high price. From this point of view, a craving is not a verdict but a wave and a question: what am I really looking for?
craving.practice: When the craving comes, name it out loud: “This is a wave.” Keep your attention on your breath and on one thought about what matters to you, until the wave begins to subside.

addiction.text: Addiction is not a moral failure but a very strong habit, and James understood this better than many. In the chapter “Habit” in The Principles of Psychology he described the nervous system as a plastic material: a repeated action wears an ever-deeper groove, and following it becomes almost automatic. This explains why it is so hard to break the cycle, and it lifts the charge of “weak will.” But the same thought gives rise to hope: plasticity works both ways, and a new groove is also worn by repetition. James advised relying on support from outside and on every small action in the right direction. And in The Varieties of Religious Experience he described with respect people who found a way out through community and a change in what they leaned on inside.
addiction.practice: Notice today one small action that is already pulling you toward a new groove, and acknowledge it. If you like, think about who could support you in this — someone close to you, or a mutual-help group.

hangover.text: A hangover is doubly hard: the body aches, and on top of that come anxiety, shame, fragments of last night. This is an understandable state, and you don't have to punish yourself right now. James reminds us that emotions are largely born from bodily sensations. When the body is dehydrated, worn out and overstimulated, it produces anxiety and gloom all by itself — and the mind readily finds explanations for them: “I've ruined everything,” “everyone is judging me.” From this point of view, much of the morning anxiety is the voice of the body, not an accurate assessment of your life. This doesn't mean last night doesn't matter. But big conclusions about yourself are better postponed until your body has recovered. For now it's enough to take care of it.
hangover.practice: Drink some water, exhale slowly and tell yourself: “Part of this feeling is my body. Conclusions can wait until tomorrow.”

euphoria.text: A burst of euphoria is bright and generous, as if the world had flung itself open. There's no need to spoil it with suspicion. James studied such highs with great interest. In The Varieties of Religious Experience he described states in which everything seems connected, important, possible — and he believed they have a value of their own: they show that ordinary everyday consciousness is only one form of experience. James was a pragmatist, so he asked a simple question: what difference does this experience make in life? From this point of view, you can not only live through euphoria but also “gather the harvest”: notice what thoughts and desires it opens up, and what of this is worth taking into ordinary days. The high will pass, but what you found can stay.
euphoria.practice: Write down one thought or desire that appeared during this high. In a couple of days, reread it and ask: what of this do I want to make real?

crash.text: A sharp drop after a high is unpleasant and often frightening: it seems the grayness is now forever. This is an understandable reaction. James helps us look at it through the body. According to his theory of emotions, a feeling is largely the sensation of a bodily state. After a strong high — a celebration, a success, a sleepless night — the body is depleted, and its tiredness is experienced as gloom and meaninglessness. From this point of view, the comedown is not a revelation that life is empty but a natural swing that will pass as you recover. James also described consciousness as a “stream”: states in it don't stand still, one flows into another. The drop is part of the stream too. You don't have to believe everything it whispers.
crash.practice: Tell yourself: “This is a comedown, not the truth about my life.” Do one simple thing for your body: eat something, drink water, take a walk.

panic.text: A wave of panic is truly frightening, and James knew this firsthand. In The Varieties of Religious Experience he included an anonymous account — it later became known that it was his own experience — of a sudden attack of terror, a “fear of my own existence,” after which he was shaken for a long time. He lived through it and went on living and working. His theory of emotions says: fear is largely the sensation of a racing heart, broken breathing, tension. That means fear can also be influenced through the body. Such a wave usually peaks and subsides within a few minutes. You don't need to defeat it now — you need to help your body pass through it: an exhale, something solid underfoot, attention to what's around you.
panic.practice: Put your feet on the floor and feel them. Several times, make your exhale slower than your inhale, and silently name five objects you can see.

dread.text: Existential dread — the question “what's the point of it all?” and the feeling of an abyss — is familiar to many deep people. James treated it with enormous respect. In The Varieties of Religious Experience he distinguished the “healthy-minded,” who don't notice the dark side of life, from the “sick soul,” who sees it keenly. And he believed the latter sees more, not less. He himself went through a severe crisis. His pragmatic answer was not consolation in words: in the lecture “Is Life Worth Living?” he said that meaning does not lie ready-made but is partly created by our participation — belief, action, care. From this point of view, dread can be acknowledged as an honest question, answered not by reasoning but by the steps of life.
dread.practice: Write down one small task in which you are needed today — by someone or something. Do it, even just a little.

fomo.text: The feeling that everyone else is living more interesting lives while you're missing the main thing is exhausting and familiar to almost everyone. James offered a very sober thought about this. In The Principles of Psychology he wrote that each of us has many possible selves: you could become a scientist, a traveler, the life of the party — but you can't become all of them at once. Choosing one means giving up the others, and this is not a defeat but a condition of life. James even said that giving up pretensions brings relief. From this point of view, the fear of missing out is the inevitable shadow of any choice. It doesn't mean you chose wrongly. It means you are a living person in a world where there are more possibilities than lives.
fomo.practice: Name one opportunity you are missing right now and quietly say: “This isn't mine for now.” Notice what has changed in your body.

sleepless.text: Insomnia and 3 a.m. thoughts are an exhausting experience, and fighting them by force rarely works. James described consciousness as a “stream”: thoughts flow by themselves, one catching on another, and they can't be stopped on command. At night, with no outside tasks, this stream becomes especially loud, and the body, according to James's theory of emotions, adds its own tension, which itself colors thoughts with anxiety. In “The Gospel of Relaxation” James advised not fighting the state but letting go of muscular tension and hurry. From this point of view, nighttime thoughts are not necessarily true: at three in the morning everything looks darker than it is. You can let the stream flow without following every thought.
sleepless.practice: Lying down, move your attention through your body from bottom to top, and with each exhale release one place: feet, belly, shoulders, jaw, forehead.

betrayal.text: Betrayal wounds deeply: the trust you leaned on collapses. This pain is warranted and legitimate. James wrote a lot about trust as a practical force: in his essay “The Will to Believe” he noted that many human bonds rest on someone being willing to trust first — and without that willingness no cooperation is possible. Betrayal shows the other side: trust is always a risk. From this point of view, your pain doesn't prove you were naive. You were doing what makes life among people possible at all. James would add: the question is not whether to trust at all, but whom and how much. That can be decided gradually, drawing on experience rather than fear.
betrayal.practice: Write one sentence: “I trusted because…” Look at it as a value of yours, not a mistake.

jealousy.text: Jealousy is a burning mixture of fear of loss, hurt and insecurity. In The Principles of Psychology James counted it among the very ancient, instinctive reactions shared by humans and animals. This helps you not to be ashamed of the feeling itself: it arises faster than we can think. But James also showed that jealousy is connected with our “social self” — with how we are seen and recognized by the people who matter to us. When it seems that recognition is going to someone else, our very self-esteem suffers. From this point of view, jealousy is less about the other person than about the fear of losing your place in someone's life. You can acknowledge this feeling without immediately turning it into action: the wave rises and falls.
jealousy.practice: Notice where you feel jealousy in your body. Tell yourself: “I'm afraid of losing my place.” Breathe with this for a minute without acting.

resentment.text: Long-held resentment is a heavy load, and almost always a real injustice stands behind it. James offered a thought that may lighten it a little. In his essay “On a Certain Blindness in Human Beings” he wrote that we are almost always blind to the inner lives of others: we don't see what matters to them, what torments them, what they live for. This blindness is mutual. The person who hurt you most likely didn't see your pain — and perhaps still doesn't. From this point of view, one could say that resentment often rests on waiting for the other person to finally understand. That waiting is understandable, but it ties you to them. Sometimes relief comes when you acknowledge your own truth yourself, without waiting for them to acknowledge it.
resentment.practice: Write a letter you don't need to send: “It hurt me because…” End with the sentence: “I acknowledge this myself.”

heartbreak.text: A broken heart is one of the sharpest pains, and it needs time. James wrote that our self is not only the body and thoughts but everything we call our own: people, home, shared plans. When someone close leaves, we lose part of our own extended self, and that is why the pain feels almost physical. This is neither exaggeration nor weakness. From this point of view, the grief of a breakup is the work of rebuilding yourself: an important part has been taken out of your self, and it takes time to find a new balance. James the pragmatist would add that the habits that connected you to the person will keep echoing for a long time — and that is normal. Gradually, new ones will take their place.
heartbreak.practice: Notice one habit that painfully reminds you of the person right now. Come up with a small new ritual for that time of day, just for yourself.

impostor.text: The fear of being found out at any moment is agonizing — and it's often familiar precisely to conscientious people. James proposed a useful formula: self-esteem depends on the ratio of successes to pretensions. The higher we set the bar, the less any real result pleases us. Impostor syndrome often grows out of inflated pretensions: it seems that a “real expert” knows everything, while you only know a lot. James wrote that we have many “social selves” — we are different for different people — and this is not deception but simply how a human being is made. He also noted that giving up unbearable pretensions brings almost as much relief as fulfilling them. From this point of view, you can allow yourself not to be perfect — and still remain yourself.
impostor.practice: Write down what you feel a “real” person in your place should be like. Which of these demands can you honestly cross out?

quote.text: To give up pretensions is as blessed a relief as to get them gratified.
quote.author: William James
quote.source: The Principles of Psychology, ch. X “The Consciousness of Self” (1890)

self_hatred.text: When an inner voice keeps insisting that you are bad and worthless, it is very painful. That voice is wrong, even if it sounds convincing. James himself went through a severe crisis and long self-criticism in his youth. His way out was not to out-argue the inner judge but a practical step: he decided to believe in his own free will and to act without waiting for the doubts to disappear. James also showed that self-esteem depends on our pretensions: if our demands on ourselves are inflated, anyone will seem a failure to themselves. From this point of view, the inner critic is not an objective voice of truth but a consequence of a bar that can be reconsidered. You don't need to love yourself first in order to take a step.
self_hatred.practice: Write down the harshest verdict of your inner critic. Below it, write what you would say to a close friend if they spoke about themselves this way.

helplessness.text: Helplessness is a heavy feeling: it seems nothing can be changed. It deserves respect, because it often reflects real limitations. James, who went through a crisis of powerlessness in his youth, came to a pragmatic conclusion: we can't know in advance whether our efforts will be enough, but some things become possible only when we act as if they were possible. In “The Will to Believe” he wrote that there are cases where faith in a result itself helps bring it about. This is not “think positive” and not a promise that everything will work out. It's an invitation to find a small area where your step changes something, and to lean on it. From this point of view, helplessness is not the end but the place where a very small action begins.
helplessness.practice: Find one action that takes less than five minutes and touches the situation at least a little. Do it and notice how the feeling has changed.

procrastination.text: “I can't get started” isn't laziness but a state everyone knows. James described it in the chapter “Will” in The Principles of Psychology with humor and sympathy. His example is a morning in a cold room: you lie there knowing it's time to get up, but your body won't obey. And suddenly, at a moment when you've been distracted from the struggle, you're already on your feet. James believed that action begins when the right thought occupies consciousness without interference — not when we force ourselves. From this point of view, procrastination doesn't need to be defeated with moral reproaches. What helps is making the needed thought simple and near: not “write the report” but “open the file.” Everything else may begin on its own.
procrastination.practice: Phrase your first step so that it takes less than a minute — for example, “open the document.” Think only about it, and do it.

uprooted.text: Being cut off from home — after a move or emigration — can be very painful: the ground under your feet disappears, along with the familiar language and the very rhythm of life. This loss is real. James explains well why it's so hard. According to his theory, a huge part of our life rests on habits: they save energy and give a sense of stability. When you move, hundreds of habits break at once, and everything that used to happen by itself now requires effort. Hence the exhausting tiredness and disorientation. James also wrote about the “social self”: we live in the recognition of people who know us, and in a new place no one knows us yet. From this point of view, your heaviness is the natural price of rebuilding. New habits and connections form gradually, one repetition at a time.
uprooted.practice: Start one small daily habit in the new place — the same walk, the same café. Notice how it becomes “yours.”

overload.text: Overload and the endless flow of information wear you out: attention is torn into pieces. This is not your inability to concentrate. James was one of the first to study attention. He wrote that attention is choice: we perceive the world only by selecting a small part of it, and it is this selection that makes experience ours. When the flow is too great, choice becomes impossible, and consciousness is swamped. James also noted that wisdom largely consists in knowing what to let pass: not everything requires a response. From this point of view, overload is not a personal failure but a signal that your choice has been taken away. You can get it back through small decisions: what I'm not reading now, what I'm not answering, what I'm leaving without attention.
overload.practice: Choose three things you can consciously skip today. Tell yourself: “I'm not taking this on.”

quote.text: The art of being wise is the art of knowing what to overlook.
quote.author: William James
quote.source: The Principles of Psychology, ch. XXII “Reasoning” (1890)

unreality.text: The feeling that the world or you yourself are somehow not real can be strange and unsettling. It's worth treating gently. James wrote about it with great attention. The Principles of Psychology has a chapter, “The Perception of Reality,” where he shows that the feeling “this is real” is not self-evident but a particular experience that can weaken. In The Varieties of Religious Experience he cited accounts of people for whom the world suddenly became distant, alien, as if behind glass, and he treated them without judgment. From James's point of view, the sense of reality is closely tied to the body and to a living interest in things. So you can return to it through sensations and simple action, without arguing with yourself.
unreality.practice: Touch a nearby surface with your palm — a table, a wall, fabric. Name three sensations out loud: temperature, texture, pressure.

awe.text: Awe and reverence before something vast or beautiful are a rare and precious experience. James studied it seriously. In The Varieties of Religious Experience he described states in which a person feels connected with something greater than themselves, and he identified their features: they are hard to put into words, and at the same time they feel like knowledge, like revelation. James was in no hurry to explain such experiences as “merely” physiology: he believed they should be judged by their fruits — by how they change a life. From this point of view, your awe is not an empty emotion but a moment when the familiar frame widens. You can simply live it and remember it.
awe.practice: Stay one more minute with whatever filled you with awe. Then try to find one word for the feeling — and notice that words fall short.

quote.text: Our normal waking consciousness, rational consciousness as we call it, is but one special type of consciousness, whilst all about it, parted from it by the filmiest of screens, there lie potential forms of consciousness entirely different.
quote.author: William James
quote.source: The Varieties of Religious Experience, Lectures XVI–XVII “Mysticism” (1902)

relief.text: Relief is a pleasant, bodily feeling: something has let go, you can breathe out. Allow yourself to feel it fully. By his theory of emotions, James would say that relief is largely the sensation of the body unclenching: the shoulders relax, breathing deepens. In The Varieties of Religious Experience he also described deeper moments of relief — when a person stops holding everything up alone and feels they can trust, let go. James considered such experiences very important: they show how much energy we usually spend on tension. From this point of view, relief is a hint: this is what your body can be like without the extra load. It's worth noticing and remembering.
relief.practice: Notice where in your body things have become lighter right now. Rest your palm there for a few breaths and simply stay with the sensation.

calm.text: Calm and peace are precious states that need no justification. In his essay “The Gospel of Relaxation” (1899), James wrote that this is exactly what many people lack: they live in constant hurry and tension, even when there is no need. According to his theory of emotions, bodily tension itself generates anxiety, and relaxation generates calm. From this point of view, calm is not laziness or inaction but a resource from which clear and strong activity is later born. James believed that calm composure works better than convulsive effort. So you can not only value your calm but also memorize it with your body, to make it easier to return to later.
calm.practice: Memorize how your shoulders, face and breathing feel right now. Come up with a short anchor word for this state.

inspiration.text: Inspiration is a vivid, living state in which strength seems to flow in. James wrote an essay about it, “The Energies of Men” (1907). He noticed that we usually use only a small part of our capacities, and he described the phenomenon of “second wind”: after the first tiredness, a new layer of energy suddenly opens up. Inspiration, from this point of view, is a moment when we touch these reserves. James didn't consider this mysticism: such powers are unlocked by strong ideas, enthusiasm, the example of other people. One could say that inspiration shouldn't be spent on worrying about where it will go. Better to give it a task — even a small one — so that the energy you've found has time to become an act.
inspiration.practice: Write down one idea that inspiration has brought, and take the first small step toward it right now.

quote.text: Compared with what we ought to be, we are only half awake.
quote.author: William James

schadenfreude.text: Schadenfreude is unpleasant to notice in yourself, but it is very human and says nothing final about you. In The Principles of Psychology James described the “social self” — how others see and recognize us — and showed that our self-esteem is largely built on comparison. His formula “self-esteem equals success divided by pretensions” also explains schadenfreude: someone else's failure seems for a moment to narrow the gap between us and who we would like to be. From this point of view, one could say that schadenfreude is a signal not of malice but of wounded self-esteem looking for a breather. James believed it's useful to treat feelings as facts of experience: notice them, name them, ask where they lead. Then schadenfreude becomes a hint — about where comparing yourself hurts.
schadenfreude.practice: Ask yourself: “In what way am I comparing myself with this person?” And name one of your pretensions that could be loosened a little.

contempt.text: Contempt is a feeling with a chill of superiority in it, and it isn't easy to admit to yourself. Don't rush to judge yourself. James wrote a short but famous essay, “On a Certain Blindness in Human Beings.” In it he says that we are almost always blind to the inner significance of other people's lives: what is full of meaning for someone else seems empty and absurd to us from the outside. He gave himself as an example: driving past poor clearings in the mountains, he saw only ugliness — and only later understood that for the settlers they were a symbol of labor and hope. From this point of view, contempt is often exactly this kind of blindness. You don't need to overcome it right away. You can simply allow that you aren't seeing everything.
contempt.practice: About the person you feel contempt for, complete the sentence: “Perhaps this matters to them because…” One guess is enough.

disgust.text: Disgust is a strong bodily feeling, and it has a right to exist. James proposed a bold theory of emotions: first we react bodily — we draw back, grimace, feel queasy — and the perception of these changes is itself the emotion. From this point of view, disgust is above all the body saying “step away.” It's an ancient protective mechanism, and it fires faster than thought. So disgust toward a person, a situation or even yourself doesn't always mean a considered judgment: the body may be reacting to a smell, a tone, a memory. James suggested noticing how expressing a feeling intensifies it. If you soften your posture and breathing a little, it sometimes becomes visible what lies behind the disgust — fear, hurt, or simply tiredness.
disgust.practice: Notice how disgust shows up in your body: face, shoulders, stomach. Gently relax one place and see what changes.

revenge.text: The desire for revenge is understandable: you've been hurt, and something inside demanding justice is looking for an outlet. This feeling doesn't make you a bad person. James wrote a great deal about how the will works. According to his idea of “ideo-motor action,” any thought that occupies consciousness tends by itself toward being carried out, if nothing counterbalances it. Will, he believed, largely comes down to what we hold our attention on. From this point of view, revenge fantasies don't mean you are “wicked”; they are a thought demanding an outlet and therefore taking up the whole field. You needn't fight it head-on — you can gently widen your attention: what else is true in this situation? What do you need right now — protection, recognition, peace?
revenge.practice: Write the revenge fantasy in one line, and under it: “What I really need is…” What is it?

anger_at_loved.text: Anger at loved ones — a partner, parents, children — is familiar to almost everyone, and so is the shame that follows. You are not a bad person because it flares up. James wrote that habits are “grooves” in the nervous system: what is repeated begins to happen by itself, before we have time to think. We spend the most time with those close to us, so it is with them that the deepest grooves of reaction form — often dating back to childhood, or coming from tiredness. From this point of view, an outburst is not a verdict on your love but a well-worn path along which a nervous impulse ran. James believed grooves can be changed little by little: not through grand promises, but through small repeated actions, started at the first opportunity.
anger_at_loved.practice: Choose one tiny new gesture for moments of irritation — an exhale, a step to the side, the words “give me a minute” — and try it today.

ambivalence.text: To love a person and at the same time be unable to stand them is a difficult but very common state. In The Varieties of Religious Experience James devoted a whole chapter to “the divided self”: he described people in whom opposing strivings coexist, and treated this with great sympathy. He also insisted on “pluralism”: reality doesn't have to reduce to a single formula, and experience can hold things that logically argue with each other. From this point of view, mixed feelings toward someone close are neither a mistake nor a sign of falseness. They reflect the fact that relationships have many layers. James believed that inner unity comes gradually, sometimes on its own, and doesn't need to be forcibly hurried.
ambivalence.practice: Tell yourself: “Both are in me, and both feelings are true.” Notice how your body responds.

guilty_relief.text: Relief after a breakup, a departure or a loved one's long illness can come with a sharp sense of guilt. But relief doesn't cancel love. James described consciousness as a “stream” in which many notes sound at once: one thought draws another after it, one feeling passes into another, and every moment has a “fringe” of vague, unnamed experiences. From this point of view, relief and grief can flow side by side without pushing each other out. James, who himself knew long periods of exhaustion, also understood how costly prolonged strain is. When it ends, body and soul breathe out, and that is natural. Your relief speaks of how much you have endured.
guilty_relief.practice: Put your hand on your chest and say: “I feel relief, and I love.” Let both sentences be true.

indifference.text: Sometimes where something “should” move you, there is silence inside. It's frightening, but it doesn't make you heartless. James knew such states well: in The Varieties of Religious Experience he described periods when the world seems “flat,” alien, drained of color, and he admitted that he himself went through a severe crisis in his youth. He stressed that this isn't a person's choice: the sense that things matter is a gift that can temporarily weaken. James also taught that emotions are largely bodily. From this point of view, indifference may simply be a sign of the organism's tiredness, not a moral flaw. You don't need to force yourself to feel the “right” way. James believed that the stream of consciousness changes, and colors have a way of coming back.
indifference.practice: Today, note one tiny thing that stirred even a shadow of response: a taste, a sound, warmth. Even a shadow counts.

escape.text: The wish to drop everything and leave — a job, a city, a role — is familiar to many. It says something important, not something weak. James called habit “the enormous fly-wheel of society”: it keeps us in our groove, which both saves and constrains us. Over the years, he wrote, a person almost grows into their profession and manners. In Pragmatism he also mentioned with sympathy “moral holidays” — the need to let go, at least for a while, of the constant strain of responsibility. From this point of view, the dream of escape is a longing for rest from the groove and for unused powers: James believed we usually live on only part of our energy. You don't have to tear your life down. You can look into what kind of freshness you are missing.
escape.practice: Give yourself a fifteen-minute “moral holiday”: do something you never do in your usual role.

quote.text: Habit is thus the enormous fly-wheel of society, its most precious conservative agent.
quote.author: William James
quote.source: The Principles of Psychology, ch. IV “Habit” (1890)

forbidden_attraction.text: Attraction to someone who is “off-limits” can be embarrassing and frightening. But the feeling itself is not yet an act or a verdict. James described “the divided self”: a state in which different strivings live in a person at the same time, and one of them seems foreign to them. He wrote about it without moralizing, as a natural part of inner life. James also showed that consciousness is a stream in which images and desires we never ordered constantly arise. From this point of view, attraction speaks rather of what your stream is looking for: novelty, attention, a different version of yourself. It's useful to ask what part of your life this feeling is telling you about. Understanding it doesn't commit you to anything.
forbidden_attraction.practice: Write: “Around them I feel…” What is that word — and where else in your life are you missing it?

social_anxiety.text: Shyness and the fear of being judged are a heavy feeling that keeps many people apart from others. James wrote that a person has as many “social selves” as there are people who know them: we are a little different with each. That's why another person's opinion touches us so sharply — it seems to create one of our selves. But James also offered a practical thought: feeling and action are more closely linked than it seems. We can't always order a feeling to vanish, but we can change our posture, voice and breathing a little — and the feeling follows. From this point of view, you don't need to wait for the fear to pass. You can take a small step together with the fear.
social_anxiety.practice: Before a conversation, square your shoulders, lower them and take a slow exhale. Don't wait for the fear to disappear — just begin.

quote.text: Action seems to follow feeling, but really action and feeling go together.
quote.author: William James

uncertainty.text: Uncertainty is exhausting: the mind wants to know how everything will end, and knowing is impossible. James is a philosopher who made uncertainty part of his view of the world. He considered the universe “pluralistic” and unfinished: the future isn't written in advance; it holds real possibilities. This is unsettling, but for James it is also where our freedom lies: since the outcome isn't predetermined, our actions really do affect something. In the essay “Is Life Worth Living?” he wrote that life always involves risk, and that our faith in a possible result sometimes itself helps bring it about. From this point of view, uncertainty is not only a threat but also a space in which your steps matter.
uncertainty.practice: Ask yourself: “What one step can I take today without knowing how everything will end?” Write it down.

quote.text: It is only by risking our persons from one hour to another that we live at all.
quote.author: William James

waiting.text: Waiting — for results, an answer, news — stretches time out agonizingly. James studied how we experience time. He noticed a paradox: a stretch of time filled with varied impressions passes quickly while it's happening but seems long in memory. Empty time, in which we only wait, drags on endlessly, yet afterward leaves almost no trace. Moreover, he wrote that waiting itself fixes our attention on the passing of time. From this point of view, the agony of waiting is not your weakness but a law of perception. And a gentle piece of advice follows from it: fill the time you spend waiting a little. Not to forget, but so as not to leave yourself alone with an empty clock face.
waiting.practice: For the next hour, choose one activity that needs the attention of your hands or eyes: cooking, a walk, drawing. Notice how time changes.

regret.text: Regret over something done or left undone can hold on for a long time. It shows what matters to you. In his lecture “The Dilemma of Determinism” James paid special attention to regret. He reasoned like this: if we regret something, we thereby admit that things could have been otherwise, that the world is not a mechanism written out in advance. Regret, for James, is evidence that people have real choice and that their actions carry weight. From this point of view, your pain speaks of freedom and responsibility, not of worthlessness. But the same thought implies: since the future is open too, regret can be turned into an understanding of how you want to act from now on.
regret.practice: Complete: “I regret…, because what matters to me is…” And: “Next time I would like to…”

longing.text: Longing for a particular person is a deep feeling, and there is nothing shameful in it. James wrote that our self is much wider than the body: it includes the people close to us, our home, everything we call “mine.” The loss or absence of someone close, in his words, is felt as the loss of a part of oneself. In addition, habit wears “grooves” in us: we get used to a voice, to gestures, to shared rituals, and when the person isn't near, these grooves go on waiting for them. From this point of view, longing is your extended self feeling an empty place. You don't have to hurry it. It shows how much this person has become part of you.
longing.practice: Recall one habit you shared with this person. Could you gently keep it as a sign of your connection?

world_pain.text: Pain for the world from hard news, violence, injustice is a sign that you are capable of compassion. James did not turn away from suffering: he wrote that the “sick soul,” which sees the evil in the world, may see reality more broadly than the cheerful optimist. But he didn't propose despair either. His position was called “meliorism”: the world should be considered neither hopelessly bad nor necessarily good — it can be made better, and every contribution matters. From this point of view, your pain needs neither to be numbed nor grown without limit. It can be turned into a small contribution, proportionate to your strength. And don't forget to rest: meliorism is a long road, not a sprint.
world_pain.practice: Choose one concrete good deed for this week. Then allow yourself an hour without news.

rejection.text: Rejection wounds deeply, and James understood well why. He wrote about the “social self” — the recognition we get from others — and considered the need to be noticed one of the strongest in a human being. That's why rejection feels almost like physical pain. But in the same chapter of The Principles of Psychology James explained that we have many social selves: each person and each group sees us in their own way. One person's rejection wounds one of these selves, but it doesn't cancel all the others. From this point of view, you can give yourself time to grieve — and remember those in whose eyes you still exist, matter and are loved.
rejection.practice: Name three people around whom you feel noticed. Could you write to one of them today?

quote.text: No more fiendish punishment could be devised, were such a thing physically possible, than that one should be turned loose in society and remain absolutely unnoticed by all the members thereof.
quote.author: William James
quote.source: The Principles of Psychology, ch. X (1890)

abandonment.text: The fear of being abandoned is a deep and painful feeling, and it deserves gentleness. In his essay “The Will to Believe,” James gave an example that touches exactly on this. Do you like me or not? he asked. The answer often depends on whether I myself am willing to take a step toward you, to believe it is possible. For James, there are truths that are created by trust: relationships hold together because each person acts in the faith that the other will also be there. From this point of view, the fear is understandable, since trust is always a risk. But it also suggests that you are not merely waiting passively to see whether you'll be left: your small steps of trust take part in creating the bond.
abandonment.practice: Today, make one small gesture of trust toward someone close — a message, a question, a thank-you — and notice what you feel as you do it.

unrequited.text: Unrequited love wounds painfully, and your pain is real. In his essay “On a Certain Blindness in Human Beings,” James wrote about a lover who sees in his beloved a charm and perfection to which indifferent onlookers remain cold. And he asked: which of them is closer to the truth? James leaned toward the view that the lover sees what is really there, and the others are blind. From this point of view, your love is not foolishness or a mistake but a special keenness of sight for another person's worth. Its going unanswered doesn't cancel this keenness. But it's important to turn the same ability to see worth toward yourself as well: you too deserve that kind of gaze.
unrequited.practice: Write down what you saw in this person. And beside it, one quality in yourself that deserves the same attention.

humiliation.text: Humiliation is one of the most painful experiences: as if you had been stripped of dignity in front of others. It is not your fault that this happened. James described “self-feeling” — the primary emotions of self-satisfaction and self-dissatisfaction — and showed how strongly they depend on the recognition of those around us. Humiliation strikes exactly there: at the “social self,” at the image in which we are seen. But James stressed that we have many social selves, and that the core of the person — the stream of consciousness, the living sense of oneself from within — belongs to no one else's gaze. From this point of view, humiliation wounds one facet of you but does not take away your self. You can give the wound time to heal.
humiliation.practice: Tell yourself: “What was done to me is not who I am.” Find a person around whom you feel your dignity.

body_shame.text: Dissatisfaction with your body is a very common and painful feeling. James wrote that the body is the “innermost part” of our material self: we experience it as ourselves, which is why any judgment of the body wounds so deeply. And his formula of self-esteem — successes divided by pretensions — suggests where part of this pain comes from: from a huge “denominator,” from expectations that are often imposed from outside. James noted that giving up some pretensions is as much a relief as achieving them. From this point of view, you needn't fight your body; you can reconsider your demands on it. The body is not a project to be graded but the one that lets you live and feel.
body_shame.practice: Name one demand on your body that you could let go of today. What does life sound like without it?

illness.text: Illness, when the body lets you down, knocks the ground out from under you. It's hard, and you have every right to be upset. James knew this firsthand: almost all his life he struggled with problems with his back, eyes and heart, and with long periods of exhaustion. And still he wrote his major books. In The Varieties of Religious Experience he wrote with respect about people who found meaning and support in the hardest circumstances. From this point of view, illness is part of human experience, not a defeat. James proposed testing ideas by how they help us live. You might ask: what thought about your illness makes this day a little easier?
illness.practice: Write down one thought that makes today a little easier for you. Reread it in the evening.

pride.text: Pride in what you've done is a healthy and deserved feeling. James considered “self-complacency” one of the primary emotions, as natural as joy. He described how it shows in the body: upright posture, ease of movement, the urge to act. From this point of view, one could say that pride is a signal from the organism: “you did it, you can.” And his formula of self-esteem — successes divided by pretensions — reminds us that the feeling of accomplishment doesn't have to be postponed until huge victories. If you've done what mattered to you, the “numerator” has grown. Let yourself enjoy this moment without comparing it to other people's successes.
pride.practice: Straighten up, take a deep breath and name out loud one thing you've done. Stay in that feeling for half a minute.

melancholy.text: Gentle sadness is a quiet feeling in which sorrow is mixed with tenderness. It doesn't need “fixing.” James distinguished two types of soul: the “healthy-minded,” which sees the world as bright, and the “sick soul,” which feels its fragility and shadow. For him the word “sick” was not a verdict. He believed that such a view may take in reality more broadly, because it doesn't turn away from loss, and that the deepest worldviews are born from contact with it. From this point of view, your melancholy is not a breakdown but a special sensitivity to what passes. James also wrote about the “stream of consciousness”: nothing in it happens twice. Perhaps gentle sadness is simply the knowledge of this.
melancholy.practice: Step outside or to a window for a couple of minutes and notice what, at this moment, is passing and will not come again.
